readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module explains how AWS networks are built, starting with Amazon VPC, subnets and the gateways that let traffic in or keep it out. It compares ways to connect remote users and on-premises sites to AWS, from Client VPN and Site-to-Site VPN to dedicated AWS Direct Connect lines, and shows how PrivateLink gives a VPC private access to services as if they were inside it. It then shows how security groups and network ACLs filter traffic, walks through building a VPC in the console, and finishes with edge services (Route 53, CloudFront, Global Accelerator) and real multi-Region designs.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 5 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Networking: what VPCs and public and private subnets are, and how to read AWS network diagrams.

Network Components in the AWS Cloud

  1. Organizing AWS Cloud Resources: VPC benefits, internet gateways, virtual private gateways with VPNs, and a first look at Direct Connect.
  2. More Ways to Connect to the AWS Cloud: Client VPN, Site-to-Site VPN, PrivateLink and Direct Connect, plus Transit Gateway, NAT gateway and API Gateway.
  3. Subnets, Security Groups, and Network Access Control Lists: how packets are filtered by stateless network ACLs and stateful security groups, and who owns that job.
  4. Amazon VPC Demo: a console walkthrough that sets up a VPC whose public and private subnets span two AZs, then gives the public ones internet access.
  5. Global Networking: edge networking, DNS, Route 53, CloudFront and Global Accelerator.

Cloud in Real Life

  1. Global Architectures: choosing VPN or Direct Connect, failover between them, and multi-Region delivery with Route 53 and CloudFront.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Amazon VPC gives you a logically isolated network in AWS, and subnets split it into public and private IP address ranges.
  • An internet gateway is the public way into a VPC, while a virtual private gateway admits encrypted VPN traffic only from approved networks.
  • Client VPN serves remote workers, Site-to-Site VPN serves offices and data centers, PrivateLink gives a VPC private access to services and other VPCs, and Direct Connect gives a dedicated, high-bandwidth line.
  • VPNs ride shared networks and can slow under load, so Direct Connect suits large transfers, steady performance and compliance, often with a VPN kept as failover.
  • Network ACLs filter at the subnet edge, are stateless and support allow and deny rules, while security groups filter per instance, are stateful and use allow rules only.
  • Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, configuring network ACLs and security groups is the customer's job.
  • A subnet becomes public only when its route table sends traffic to an attached internet gateway.
  • DNS turns domain names into IP addresses, and Route 53 adds routing policies, health checks and domain registration on top.
  • CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users, and Global Accelerator gives static IPs and health-aware routing over the AWS global network with fast failover.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The recap starts with the core building blocks: a VPC to keep your workload isolated, plus gateways, security groups and network ACLs to control what moves in and out. For reaching AWS from your own sites, you can pick a VPN, which encrypts traffic across the shared public internet, or Direct Connect, a private connection nobody else uses. Finally, edge services bring content and lookups close to users, with Route 53 handling DNS and CloudFront keeping cached copies near consumers.

Introduction to Networking

Objectives

  • Explain the purpose of a VPC.
  • Explain the purpose of a .
  • Tell public subnets apart from private ones.

Notes

Networking and the coffee shop

  • links devices to share data and resources, and in AWS it means the infrastructure and services hosting your workloads.
  • Coffee shop: cashiers face customers as public resources, while baristas stay private.

Amazon VPC and subnets

  • gives you a logically isolated part of the AWS Cloud with a virtual network you design.
  • Public resources can reach the internet and private ones cannot.
  • Subnets organize resources, share some publicly (a website) and keep others isolated and private (a customer database).
  • from discrete data centers is an trait, not a subnet one.

Reading network diagrams

  • A diagram is a map and blueprint that shows at a glance whether a network is redundant, secure and scalable.
  • Boxes nest from the outside in: AWS Cloud, Region (a separate geographic area picked for latency, compliance, data residency, services and cost), then the VPC as a solid box.
  • The VPC is your isolated network, where you control resources and security.
  • AZs sit side by side in a Region, each one or more data centers in separate facilities with redundant power and networking, so using several protects apps if one location fails.
  • Subnets are IP address ranges that split the VPC, drawn solid when private and dashed when public (reached through an ).

Visuals

  • Components timeline: buildings feeding a padlocked cloud with a VPC, then the VPC split into two subnets.
  • Diagram slides: the full map (a user entering via an internet gateway to two public and two private subnets over two AZs), then rebuilt layer by layer.

Key takeaways

  • A VPC is your own logically isolated network in the AWS Cloud.
  • Subnets organize resources into public (internet-facing) and private (internal) ranges.
  • Resilience to a failed location comes from multiple AZs, not from subnets.

Scenarios

  • A knowledge check practiced naming what subnets are for, apart from what AZs provide.

Terms

  • Networking: devices linked to exchange data and resources.
  • Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC): an isolated slice of the AWS Cloud with a virtual network you define.
  • Subnet: a block of VPC IP addresses used to group resources.
  • Public subnet: a subnet reaching the internet through an internet gateway.
  • Private subnet: a subnet hidden from the public internet.
  • Network diagram: a picture of how users and apps reach your AWS resources.

organizing-aws-cloud-resources.html:
Organizing AWS Cloud Resources

Objectives

  • Explain the role of a .
  • Name the core building blocks of a VPC.
  • Explain the role of an .

Notes

Grouping resources in a VPC

  • A VPC is your private network in AWS, with a private IP range you choose for resources such as EC2 instances and load balancers.
  • Resources go into specific subnets, chunks of the VPC's IP addresses that, together with networking rules, make them public or private.
  • Public suits internet-facing items like a website or , and private suits internal items like an HR app or backend database.
  • Without boundaries, traffic would flow unchecked among the millions of resources AWS customers run.

Amazon VPC benefits

  • Increased security: protect and watch connections, filter traffic and limit who can reach instances.
  • Control: you decide where resources sit, how they connect and how they are secured.
  • Convenience: less time spent building, running and checking the network than on premises.

Internet gateway

  • An internet gateway joins a VPC to the internet, and you must attach one before public traffic can flow in or out.
  • Attaching alone is not enough, since public subnets also need a route to it (Amazon VPC Demo).
  • Coffee shop: it is the front door, and without it no customer can get in.
  • The assessment adds that it is a managed, highly available VPC part that scales horizontally and carries traffic both ways.

Virtual private gateway and VPN

  • A VPC with only private resources skips the internet gateway and uses a virtual private gateway, which admits traffic only from an approved network.
  • The internet is like the public road to the coffee shop, and a is an encrypted tunnel along it that hides your traffic from ISPs and snoopers.
  • The virtual private gateway is the AWS-side piece that lets this protected traffic into the VPC from your own or company network.
  • Coffee shop: the shop now sits inside a corporate office building, and you must badge in before buying coffee.

VPN versus AWS Direct Connect

  • Trade-off: a VPN is encrypted but shares a network with others, so heavy use can slow it.
  • gives you your own private fiber line from the data center to the VPC, adding steady high performance to security.
  • A local Direct Connect partner installs the line, which also helps with compliance and bandwidth limits.
  • Course analogy: a VPN is like reaching the shop through a crowded shared office tower, while Direct Connect is a private door straight in.

Telling the acronyms apart

  • VPC: draws a boundary around your resources.
  • Virtual private gateway: lets protected traffic enter the VPC.
  • VPN: encrypts traffic against interception or monitoring.

Visuals

  • Organizing resources image: a company sending traffic into a VPC of AWS resources inside a boundary.
  • VPC benefits image: icons for security, time savings and control.
  • Internet gateway image: a client reaching EC2 instances through the gateway attached to the VPC.
  • Virtual private gateway image: oddly, an internet gateway picture (a client, the gateway, one subnet of three EC2 instances).
  • Acronym flashcards: VPC, virtual private gateway and VPN cards for separating look-alike names.

Key takeaways

  • Subnets plus networking rules decide whether resources are public or private.
  • brings security, control and convenience.
  • An internet gateway is required for any internet traffic to reach the VPC.
  • A virtual private gateway with a VPN gives an encrypted link that only approved private networks can use.
  • VPNs share network capacity, while Direct Connect gives a dedicated line for steady performance, bandwidth and compliance.

Scenarios

  • A knowledge check practiced the secure, isolated data center link: a virtual private gateway and VPN in front of private subnets.
  • Why the other paths fail: an internet gateway adds no protection, public subnets isolate nothing, and a VPC without subnets cannot isolate resources at all.

Terms

  • Internet gateway: the component that connects a VPC to the internet.
  • Virtual private gateway: the AWS-side component that lets protected traffic from approved networks into a VPC.
  • Virtual private network (VPN): an encrypted tunnel across the internet that hides your traffic.
  • AWS Direct Connect: a dedicated private physical link between your data center and AWS.

More Ways to Connect to the AWS Cloud

Notes

AWS Client VPN

  • For people: a fully managed, elastic linking remote staff (and on-premises networks) to AWS that scales with demand.
  • It needs no hardware or user-count guessing and adds strong authentication.
  • It runs on an OpenVPN-based client over the AWS global network.

AWS Site-to-Site VPN

  • For sites: encrypted links from data centers or branch offices to your VPC, with , private sessions and faster apps.
  • It suits app migration and remote-location links, and wins when no dedicated line or extra bandwidth is needed.

AWS PrivateLink

  • For resources: highly available, scalable private access from a VPC to services as if they were inside it, including other VPCs, other clouds and on-premises networks.
  • It needs no public IP, NAT device, , VPN or Direct Connect, and you pick exactly what is reachable, so traffic stays protected and rules simple.

AWS Direct Connect

  • Shared links can jam, so Direct Connect gives a dedicated private line from your network to a VPC (via a and a ), cutting costs and raising bandwidth.
  • Fits: latency-sensitive apps like video streaming (no internet hop), huge transfers (analytics, backups, broadcast media) and hybrid apps across AWS and on premises.
  • Choose it only when you need the bandwidth, since plain site links suit Site-to-Site VPN.

Other gateways

  • : a central hub for VPCs and on-premises networks, with inter-Region peering between transit gateways.
  • : private instances can start outside connections, but outsiders cannot start ones to them.
  • : creates APIs at any scale and publishes, secures, monitors and maintains them.

Visuals

  • Connection options image: a VPC linked to remote staff, a and an office.
  • Client VPN image: remote workers around a globe.
  • Site-to-Site VPN image: three sites joined to a virtual private gateway by VPN.
  • Direct Connect image: the dedicated path from a data center into a VPC.
  • Direct Connect accordion icons: fast media, data moving to the cloud, hybrid lines.
  • Connectivity flashcards: PrivateLink and Client VPN fronts are swapped, so trust the backs.
  • Knowledge check image: a data center on a VPN to a VPC.

Key takeaways

  • People need Client VPN, sites need Site-to-Site VPN, and private access to services or VPCs needs PrivateLink.
  • Direct Connect is the dedicated high-bandwidth link, worth it only when you need that bandwidth.
  • Transit Gateway is a hub, a NAT gateway lets private instances call out but not be called, and Gateway manages APIs.

Scenarios

  • An acquired remote workforce needs secure access fast: Client VPN.
  • Knowledge check, heavy migration that stays hybrid: Direct Connect, as the VPN options lack bandwidth.
  • Knowledge check, only protected traffic from approved networks: a virtual private gateway, not Transit Gateway or API Gateway.

Terms

  • AWS Client VPN: managed VPN for remote users.
  • AWS Site-to-Site VPN: encrypted site-to-VPC link.
  • AWS PrivateLink: private VPC access to services as if local.
  • Direct Connect location: the entry point to the Direct Connect path.
  • AWS Transit Gateway: hub for VPCs and on-premises networks.
  • NAT gateway: lets private instances call out but blocks calls in.
  • API (application programming interface): how software systems agree to interact.
  • Amazon API Gateway: service for building and managing APIs.

subnets-security-groups-and-network-acce.html:
Subnets, Security Groups, and Network Access Control Lists

Objectives

  • Explain how traffic moves through a VPC.
  • Explain how security groups filter traffic and why that makes them stateful.
  • Explain how network ACLs filter traffic and why that makes them stateless.
  • State who secures subnets with these controls under the .

Notes

Security inside the VPC

  • Gateways guard the edge of the VPC, yet perimeter defense is only one slice of network security.
  • AWS also offers tools for other layers, among them firewalls, encryption and DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) protection, which the course's security section covers later.
  • This lesson looks inward at two flexible traffic controls: network ACLs and security groups.

Subnets

  • A subnet groups resources by security or operational needs and is either public or private.
  • Public subnets hold what the public must reach, such as an online store's website.
  • Private subnets hold what only your private network should reach, such as a database of customer details and order histories.
  • A main reason to have subnets is to decide who gets to the gateways: public subnets can use the , private ones cannot.
  • Rules can let subnets talk to each other, for example public EC2 instances querying private databases.

Packets and the subnet check

  • A is one unit of data on a network, and a customer's request arrives as packets through the internet gateway.
  • Each packet crossing a subnet edge, in either direction, is judged by that subnet's on who sent it and how it is trying to communicate.
  • The check looks only at whether the sender is approved, never at what the packet carries.

Network ACLs

  • Picture the network ACL as the subnet's border guard: a virtual firewall judging everything that enters or leaves the whole subnet.
  • Analogy: airport passport control inspects travelers (packets) on arrival and on departure, turning away anyone missing from the approved list or named on a banned list.
  • Every AWS account comes with a that lets everything through until you edit its rules.
  • A starts the other way round: nothing passes until you add allow rules.
  • Each network ACL also ends in an that rejects any packet no other rule matched.
  • Stateless: it has no memory, so even the reply to a request that already left is checked from scratch.
  • Its inbound and outbound lists are separate and may differ, so being admitted does not guarantee the reply can leave.
  • Blind spot: it works only at the subnet edge, so per-instance decisions are beyond it.

Security groups

  • Instances in one subnet may need different rules about who may contact them and on which ports, which calls for instance-level control.
  • A is the instance's own virtual firewall, filtering traffic to and from one resource such as an , and every instance gets one at launch.
  • Out of the box it blocks every inbound port and sender address and lets all outbound traffic go.
  • You open it with allow rules, such as accepting only on a web server, with separate inbound and outbound rules, and anything not allowed stays blocked.
  • Analogy: a building's door attendant checks the guest list as people arrive but lets them leave without looking.
  • Stateful: it remembers an outgoing request and lets the matching reply back in whatever the inbound rules say.
  • Instances in one VPC can share a security group or each use their own.

A packet's round trip

  • Instance A in subnet 1 sends a packet to instance B in subnet 2 of the same VPC.
  • Outbound leg: A's security group lets it out by default, subnet 1's network ACL applies its own outbound list no matter what the security group decided, then subnet 2's network ACL and B's security group check it on the way in.
  • Return leg: B's security group passes the reply because it saw the request, both network ACLs consult their lists again, and A's security group lets the reply in unchecked.
  • All these checks are built into AWS networking and happen without noticeable delay.

Security groups versus network ACLs

Aspect Security groups Network ACLs
Works on Individual EC2 instances Whole subnets
Memory Stateful Stateless
Rules Allow only Allow and deny
Replies Let through automatically when the request was allowed Need rules permitting them in each direction
Best for Fine-grained, per-instance control Broad control at the subnet edge

Shared responsibility

  • Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, setting up network ACLs and security groups for your subnets and resources is your job.
  • That is , the traffic protection around your own applications.
  • AWS owns , meaning the software, hardware, data centers and facilities behind its services.

Visuals

  • Subnets diagram: a VPC with an internet gateway, a of EC2 instances and a of databases, showing the public and private split.
  • Packet permission image: the network ACL stopping an arriving packet at the subnet edge, showing where subnet checks happen.
  • Default network ACL cartoon: passport officers waving everyone in and out, the default allow-all setting.
  • Custom network ACL cartoon: officers checking a custom list both ways, showing deny-until-allowed and the catch-all deny rule.
  • Stateless cartoon: the network ACL rechecking a packet it has already seen.
  • Security group guard cartoons: guards blocking all entry but never checking exits, the default inbound-deny, outbound-allow setting.
  • Stateful cartoon: the security group recognizing a returning packet and skipping its rules.
  • Shared responsibility image: a reminder that these controls are the customer's to configure.

Key takeaways

  • Network ACLs work at the subnet level, are stateless, and support both allow and deny rules.
  • Security groups work at the instance level, are stateful, support allow rules only, and by all inbound and allow all outbound traffic.
  • The default network ACL allows everything, a custom one denies everything until you add rules, and an explicit deny rule catches unmatched packets.
  • A packet between subnets passes both security groups and both network ACLs, and only the network ACLs recheck the return trip.
  • Configuring security groups and network ACLs is the customer's responsibility, as part of security in the cloud.

Scenarios

  • An online store's website in a public subnet with customer data in a private subnet: subnets split by security needs.
  • A web server that should accept only HTTPS: a security group rule.
  • Several instances in one subnet needing different port rules: instance-level security groups.
  • Knowledge checks practiced picking a control for fine-grained per-instance rules and naming the stateless filter.

Terms

  • Packet: a unit of data traveling across a network.
  • Network access control list (network ACL): a subnet-level virtual firewall that filters traffic entering and leaving the subnet.
  • Default network ACL: the network ACL every AWS account has, which allows all traffic until modified.
  • Custom network ACL: a network ACL you create, which denies all traffic until you add allow rules.
  • Explicit deny rule: the final network ACL rule that rejects any packet not matched by another rule.
  • Stateless packet filtering: checking every packet in both directions with no memory of earlier traffic.
  • Security group: an instance-level virtual firewall for a resource such as an EC2 instance.
  • Stateful packet filtering: remembering earlier decisions so replies to allowed requests pass automatically.

amazon-vpc-demo.html:
Amazon VPC Demo

Objectives

  • Move around the .
  • Follow the steps for creating a VPC.
  • Create public and private subnets.
  • Create an and attach it to the VPC.
  • Create a , add a and associate it with the public subnets.

Notes

What the demo builds

  • In the AWS Management Console, the demo creates a VPC and four subnets (two public, two private) over two AZs, then attaches an internet gateway and routes the public side to it.
  • You may never build a VPC yourself, and the narrator says not to memorize the clicks, so focus on what each piece does.

Step 1: Create the VPC

  • Type "VPC" in the console search bar, open the VPC dashboard and choose Create VPC with the "VPC only" option, named My VPC.
  • Enter a , also called a CIDR block, which sets the pool of private IP addresses resources in the VPC can be given.
  • The demo uses the IPv4 range 10.0.0.0/16, so every resource gets a unique private address beginning with 10.0.
  • This is also when you settle on the Region best placed for your resources.

Step 2: Create the subnets

  • Placing subnets in two AZs is a best practice for , keeping instances reachable if one AZ suffers an outage.
  • In the navigation pane on the left, open Subnets in the Virtual private cloud group, then Create subnet and pick My VPC.
  • Private-subnet-1 goes in us-east-1a with 10.0.1.0/24, and the second uses another AZ and 10.0.2.0/24.
  • Under Actions, Edit subnet settings, auto-assign public IP stays off for private subnets, since turning it on would hand every resource there a public IP.
  • Public-subnet-1 goes in us-east-1a with 10.0.3.0/24, and the second uses another AZ and 10.0.4.0/24.
  • In the same settings, is switched on for public subnets so their resources receive public addresses.
  • Naming a subnet "public" does not make it public, because it still needs an attached internet gateway and a route to it.

Step 3: Create and attach the internet gateway

  • Open Internet gateways in the navigation pane, create one named my-ig, then use Actions, Attach to VPC to join it to My VPC.
  • Attaching alone does not yet tell instances how to reach the internet.

Step 4: Route the public traffic

  • A route table holds rules, called routes, that decide where network traffic is sent, and every subnet must be associated with one.
  • Open Route tables in the navigation pane and create public-route-table in My VPC.
  • Its Routes tab starts with a single local route that keeps traffic inside the VPC.
  • Choose Edit routes, then Add route, with destination 0.0.0.0/0 and the internet gateway as target.
  • On the Subnet associations tab, explicitly associate both public subnets with this table.
  • The public subnets now reach the internet through the gateway, while the private subnets lack that route and stay private.

What comes next

  • Next comes traffic filtering through security groups and network ACLs, and security groups reuse CIDR notation to define where traffic may come from or go to.
  • Finally, launch resources such as EC2 instances or databases into the subnets.

Visuals

  • Build timeline: three steps growing one diagram, from nested AWS Cloud, Region and VPC boxes, to four subnets over two AZs, to a user reaching resources through the internet gateway.

Key takeaways

  • The build order is VPC with a CIDR range, subnets across two AZs, internet gateway, route table, then security and resources.
  • A subnet only becomes public when its associated route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an attached internet gateway.
  • Auto-assign public IPv4 belongs on public subnets only.
  • At this level, know what each component does rather than the console clicks.

Scenarios

  • Instances must stay reachable if one AZ has an outage: spread subnets across two AZs.
  • A gateway is attached but instances still cannot reach the internet: add the 0.0.0.0/0 route and associate the subnets.

Terms

  • AWS Management Console: the AWS interface where you find services (for example through its search bar) and create and configure resources such as VPCs.
  • CIDR (classless inter-domain routing) range: the notation that defines a block of IP addresses, such as 10.0.0.0/16 for a VPC.
  • Auto-assign public IPv4 address: a subnet setting that gives every resource launched in it a public IPv4 address.
  • Route table: a set of routes, associated with subnets, that controls where their traffic is directed.
  • Route: a single route table rule, such as sending 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an internet gateway.

Global Networking

Objectives

  • Explain what the does.
  • Describe the benefits and uses of .
  • Describe the benefits and uses of .
  • Explain and where fits.

Notes

Edge networking

  • Edge networking pushes compute and storage toward where data is created and used, giving user-facing apps secure, speedy networking.
  • Processing or caching near users lowers latency and keeps the organization in control of its infrastructure.
  • Route 53 is one of many services hosted at the edge, building on edge locations from an earlier module.

DNS

  • DNS is the internet's phone book, turning names people read into IP (Internet Protocol) addresses computers use.
  • Resolution: the browser hands the name to a , which asks the company's DNS server, which replies with the IP address (192.0.2.0 for AnyCompany).

Amazon Route 53

  • Route 53 is a reliable, low-cost DNS service whose worldwide, auto-scaling DNS servers route users to apps in AWS (EC2 instances, load balancers) or outside it.
  • Routing policies: weighted , latency-based, geolocation and geoproximity.
  • Geolocation routes by where the customer is, so North America goes to a North American Region and Ireland to the Dublin Region.
  • It also runs health checks, registers new domains and takes over DNS records from other registrars, so all your domains live in one place.

Amazon CloudFront

  • CloudFront is a (content delivery network) that securely serves static and dynamic web content from edge locations near customers, for faster loads, lower cost and reliability.
  • Analogy: a global truck fleet parks copies of your content in local depots, so requests stop trekking to the single main warehouse (your ).
  • Example: a Seattle visitor to a site hosted in Oregon gets its images and GIFs from CloudFront's Seattle location, and shorter trips mean faster delivery.
  • Use cases: smooth workout videos at peak hours, fast store pages in busy seasons (fewer abandoned carts) and quick map loads in a travel app.

Route 53 and CloudFront together

  • Route 53 resolves AnyCompany's domain to 192.0.2.0, the request goes to the nearest CloudFront , and CloudFront hands it to an that passes it to an .

AWS Global Accelerator

  • Global Accelerator moves app traffic off crowded public routes onto the AWS private global network for better availability, performance and security.
  • The assessment adds static IP addresses and a best-endpoint choice based on endpoint health, user location and your policies.
  • Fast failover when one app location fails is the clue that separates it from Route 53 (DNS, domains, health checks) and CloudFront (content caching).
  • Use cases: even gameplay for gamers in Tokyo, London and New York, and a banking app that stays fast at peaks or on poor local networks.

Visuals

  • DNS process graphic: three markers tracing a lookup from laptop to resolver to company DNS server.
  • CloudFront trucks image: trucks hauling content around a globe.
  • Route 53 and CloudFront graphic: four markers from customer to Route 53, an edge location, a and EC2.
  • Edge services flashcards: one card each for Route 53, CloudFront and Global Accelerator.

Key takeaways

  • Edge networking brings computing and storage near users to cut latency.
  • DNS maps domain names to IP addresses through a resolver and a DNS server.
  • Route 53 resolves names, routes with policies, runs health checks, and registers or consolidates domains.
  • CloudFront caches static and dynamic content at edge locations near users.
  • Global Accelerator offers static IPs and health-aware routing over the AWS global network with fast failover.

Scenarios

  • Gamers and banking customers worldwide needing low lag: Global Accelerator.
  • Knowledge checks practiced picking a CDN for global training media and a DNS service to consolidate domains.

Terms

  • Edge networking: placing compute and storage near data sources and users.
  • Domain Name System (DNS): the system that translates website names into IP addresses.
  • DNS resolution: turning a domain name into an IP address.
  • Customer DNS resolver: takes the browser's lookup and queries the company DNS server.
  • Amazon Route 53: the AWS DNS service, highly available and scalable.
  • Routing policy: a Route 53 rule for picking an endpoint.
  • Amazon CloudFront: the AWS CDN service.
  • Content delivery network (CDN): a network serving copies of content from near users.
  • AWS Global Accelerator: carries app traffic on the AWS global network to healthy endpoints.
  • Application Load Balancer: here, passes requests from CloudFront to EC2.

Global Architectures

Objectives

  • Recognize when a fits and when Direct Connect fits.
  • Describe how a VPC uses a VPN connection and Direct Connect together.
  • Describe how CloudFront and Route 53 support a .

Notes

Beyond one VPC

  • Global firms often run many accounts, Regions and VPCs, even hybrid setups, and these diagrams are for context, not mastery.

VPN or Direct Connect

  • The common starting point is a VPC reached by VPN, an encrypted tunnel over the public internet that remote staff often use for sensitive data in AWS.
  • Weak spots: it shares the local internet link, so big data loads can drag, and strict compliance or regulatory needs may favor Direct Connect.
  • Direct Connect runs traffic from the via a and a into the VPC on a private dedicated path.
  • Payoff: faster bulk transfers, better app performance and safer data movement.
  • Rule of thumb: VPN for flexible secure remote access, modest transfers or no need for a dedicated line, and Direct Connect for big on-premises-to-AWS transfers needing far more bandwidth.

Using both: failover and aggregation

  • Direct Connect is a physical cable that can be cut, so a VPN often stands by as its , or a second Direct Connect line does.
  • Several connections can also be bundled for more total (aggregate) bandwidth.
  • Course example: customer clients and servers go through a content router or firewall and several Direct Connect links to a virtual private gateway, reaching private VPC resources securely.

Content across Regions

  • For worldwide users, CloudFront serves content from global edge locations, and Route 53 aims for the lowest latency by sending each user to the closest Region.
  • Flow: the custom domain hits a Route 53 record, a picks the nearest Region, the user goes to its CloudFront , and that location gets content from the Region's .
  • The site spans several AZs for , with an in front of an of EC2 instances.

Visuals

  • Direct Connect failover diagram: one customer network tied to a two-subnet VPC by several Direct Connect links, for redundancy and .
  • Multi-Region delivery diagram: Route 53, CloudFront, a and an Auto Scaling group in sequence, for reaching the closest Region.

Key takeaways

  • A VPN is a flexible encrypted tunnel for remote access and small transfers, but it shares bandwidth.
  • Direct Connect is a dedicated private line for large transfers, consistent performance and compliance.
  • A VPN or a second Direct Connect line can provide failover, and multiple connections add bandwidth.
  • Route 53 latency-based routing plus CloudFront edge locations give low latency across Regions.

Scenarios

  • Remote employees need sensitive data in AWS: a VPN connection.
  • A Direct Connect cable is cut: fail over to a VPN or a second Direct Connect line.
  • Offices worldwide need fast content: CloudFront with Route 53.
  • A knowledge check practiced choosing a dedicated, compliant link for heavy, sensitive data.

Terms

  • Multi-Region architecture: a design spreading an application across several Regions and VPCs.
  • Failover: switching to a backup connection when the primary one fails.
  • Aggregate bandwidth: the combined capacity of several Direct Connect connections used together.
  • Latency-based routing: a Route 53 policy that aims to give users the lowest latency, here by sending them to the closest Region.
  • Origin server: the Region's server that a CloudFront edge location pulls content from.

options.text: Latency-based routing
options.why: Latency-based routing picks whichever endpoint answers fastest, not the one tied to the customer's country.

options.text: Weighted round robin routing
options.why: Weighted round robin splits traffic by set shares and ignores where each customer is.

options.text: Geolocation routing
options.why: Geolocation routing chooses the endpoint by where the customer is, such as Ireland going to Dublin.

options.text: Geoproximity routing
options.why: Geoproximity weighs the distance between users and resources rather than the country the user is in.

questions.takeaway: Route 53 answers DNS lookups and can point users at apps running in AWS or hosted outside AWS.

read.text: Route 53 is a reliable, low-cost DNS service whose worldwide, auto-scaling DNS servers route users to apps in AWS (EC2 instances, load balancers) or outside it.

questions.stem: The cafe's online shop runs on Amazon EC2 instances, while its gift-card site still sits with an outside hosting company. The cafe wants one service to answer name lookups for both sites and send each customer to the right one. Which service fits?

options.why: A load balancer spreads requests across targets inside one Region and does not answer name lookups for the sites.

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway
options.why: A transit gateway joins VPCs and on-premises networks, and it does not resolve names for customers.

options.text: Amazon Route 53
options.why: Route 53 is a DNS service that can route users to apps running in AWS or to apps hosted outside it.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.why: Global Accelerator steers app traffic over the AWS network to endpoints, but it is not the service that answers DNS lookups.

read.text: It also runs health checks, registers new domains and takes over DNS records from other registrars, so all your domains live in one place.

options.text: Register the domain name that guests will type

options.why: Holding copies of photos at edge locations near guests is CloudFront caching, not a DNS job.

options.text: Check whether each server still answers requests
options.why: Route 53 runs health checks so it can stop pointing guests at a server that no longer answers.

options.text: Carry traffic over the AWS private global network
options.why: Moving app traffic off public routes onto the AWS private global network is what Global Accelerator does.

options.text: Run the code that sends confirmation emails
options.why: Running application code is a compute job for a service such as AWS Lambda, not something the DNS service does.

options.text: It keeps cached copies of content at edge locations
options.why: Caching content at edge locations describes CloudFront, not Global Accelerator.

options.text: It translates domain names into numeric IP addresses
options.why: Translating names into addresses is DNS work, which Route 53 handles.

options.text: It carries traffic over the private AWS network
options.why: Global Accelerator moves traffic off crowded public routes onto the AWS private global network.

options.text: It spreads requests across instances in one Region
options.why: Spreading requests inside one Region is load balancing, not the global routing Global Accelerator offers.

options.text: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnel

options.text: An AWS Client VPN endpoint
options.why: Client VPN gives remote users encrypted access over the internet, not a private dedicated path for the plant.

options.text: An AWS Transit Gateway hub
options.why: A transit gateway joins networks at one hub, but it adds no second physical path if the plant's only line is cut.

options.text: A second Direct Connect line

read.text: Direct Connect is a physical cable that can be cut, so a VPN often stands by as its failover, or a second Direct Connect line does.

questions.stem: The cafe's roasting plant sends its order data to a VPC over a single AWS Direct Connect line. The owners worry that a road crew could cut that cable one day. What can stand by so the plant still reaches the VPC if the line goes down?

options.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
options.why: An encrypted VPN tunnel from the plant to the VPC can carry the traffic while the cut Direct Connect line is repaired.

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway
options.why: A transit gateway is a hub joining networks, but it is not itself a second path from the plant if the only line is cut.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.why: Global Accelerator speeds application traffic for users to endpoints, not a backup link from the plant's data center.

options.text: A NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections, so it gives the plant no path into the VPC.

read.text: Direct Connect is a physical cable that can be cut, so a VPN often stands by as its failover, or a second Direct Connect line does.

questions.stem: A company links its data center to a VPC with several AWS Direct Connect connections instead of just one. What does it gain from the extra connections? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The lines keep traffic flowing if one of them fails

options.why: Connections used together add up to a larger aggregate bandwidth than any single line gives.

options.why: A single Direct Connect line is already a private dedicated path, so this is not something the extra lines add.

labs.title: Why can't customers reach the menu?

In this lab, customers use HTTPS on port 443 and staff use SSH on port 22, the network ACL tries its rules from the lowest number up, and each reply leaves on a high port from 1024 to 65535 (a lab value), which the network ACL checks again while the security group lets it out on its own.

cases.label: A customer opens the menu over HTTPS
The back office signs in over SSH

goals.label: Customers load the menu and get the page back

notes.title: Subnets, Security Groups, and Network Access Control Lists

lines: The security group is stateful, so once it lets the customer's request in, the page goes back out without an outbound rule.
The network ACL is stateless, so its outbound list must allow the reply even though its inbound list admitted the request.
The network ACL lets SSH into the whole subnet, so the security group's narrow back office rule decides who reaches this one server.

questions.takeaway: A stateless filter checks every reply from scratch, so a reply needs its own matching rule to leave the subnet.

read.text: Stateless: it has no memory, so even the reply to a request that already left is checked from scratch.

questions.stem: The network ACL on the cafe's menu subnet admits a customer's request on its inbound list. Nothing on its outbound list matches the reply. What happens to the reply?

options.text: It leaves because the request was admitted
options.why: A stateless filter keeps no memory of the request, so admission earns the reply nothing.

options.text: It leaves because outbound traffic is open
options.why: A network ACL checks outbound packets against its own list, and here nothing matches the reply.

options.text: It is rejected by the final deny rule
options.why: The reply is checked from scratch, and the final explicit deny rule rejects it when no rule matches.

options.text: It is held until the security group decides
options.why: The network ACL decides on its own lists, whatever the security group allows.

questions.takeaway: A stateful security group remembers allowed requests, so their replies return without matching an inbound rule.

read.text: Stateful: it remembers an outgoing request and lets the matching reply back in whatever the inbound rules say.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering instance sends a request to a supplier's price service. Its security group has no inbound rule that matches the supplier's reply. What happens to the reply at the security group?

options.text: It is let in because the request was remembered
options.why: A stateful security group remembers the outgoing request and lets its reply in whatever the inbound rules say.

options.text: It is blocked because no inbound rule matches
options.why: That would be a stateless check, but the security group recognizes the reply to its own request.

options.text: It is blocked until an explicit deny rule is removed
options.why: Security groups support allow rules only, so there is no deny rule to remove.

options.text: It is let in only if the packet content is approved
options.why: The security group does not read packet content; it passes the reply because it saw the request.

questions.takeaway: When instances in one subnet need different port rules, use security groups, which work per instance.

read.text: Instances in one subnet may need different rules about who may contact them and on which ports, which calls for instance-level control.

questions.stem: The cafe's web server and its reporting server sit in the same subnet. The web server should accept only HTTPS, while the reporting server needs a different port open. Which control lets the cafe set these rules separately for each server?

options.text: A network ACL
options.why: A network ACL applies to the whole subnet, so it cannot give two instances in it different rules.

options.text: A security group
options.why: A security group filters traffic for one instance, so each server can have its own port rules.

options.text: An internet gateway
options.why: An internet gateway links the VPC to the internet and holds no per-server port rules.

options.text: A NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outside connections and does not set port rules per server.

Place each piece so customers reach the menu, nobody outside reaches the orders, either zone can fail, and nothing unneeded runs. In this lab, the internet reaches a piece only when its subnet holds a route table to the internet gateway on the VPC edge, and the VPC and subnet address ranges are lab values.

pieces.label: Route table A

pieces.label: Route table B
pieces.detail: Local route plus 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway

goals.label: Customers reach both menu web servers
goals.hint: Follow a customer's request in, and ask what joins the VPC to the internet and what tells a subnet to send traffic there.

goals.label: Nobody outside reaches the order database

More Ways to Connect to the AWS Cloud

lines: Attaching an internet gateway is not enough, since a subnet turns public only when its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to it.
The order database sits in private subnets with no route to the internet gateway, so nobody outside can reach it.

questions.takeaway: Customers reach servers in a public subnet through the internet gateway attached to the VPC.

read.text: A subnet only becomes public when its associated route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an attached internet gateway.

questions.stem: A customer at home opens the cafe's menu site on a phone. The site runs on servers launched in a public subnet of the cafe's VPC. Through which component does the customer's request come in to reach those servers?

options.text: A NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outside connections and blocks connections started from outside, so it cannot carry this request in.

options.text: A virtual private gateway
options.why: A virtual private gateway admits protected traffic from approved networks, not requests from any customer's phone.

options.text: An internet gateway
options.why: Public subnet resources are reached from the web through the internet gateway attached to the VPC, which their route points at.

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway
options.why: Transit Gateway is a hub joining VPCs and on-premises networks, not the entry point for a customer browsing the menu site.

questions.takeaway: A private subnet keeps auto-assign public IP off and has no route to the internet gateway.

read.text: Under Actions, Edit subnet settings, auto-assign public IP stays off for private subnets, since turning it on would hand every resource there a public IP.

questions.stem: The cafe's customer database must sit in a private subnet that the internet cannot reach. How should that subnet be set up?

options.text: Keep auto-assign public IP off and leave out a route to the internet gateway
options.why: With no public addresses and no route to the gateway, the database has no path to or from the internet.

options.text: Turn auto-assign public IP on and leave out a route to the internet gateway
options.why: Switching the setting on hands every resource a public address, which a private subnet avoids.

options.text: Keep auto-assign public IP off and add a route to the internet gateway
options.why: A route to the gateway is what gives a subnet its path to the internet, so the database would no longer be private.

options.text: Turn auto-assign public IP on and add a route to the internet gateway
options.why: Both choices together build a public subnet, the opposite of what the database needs.

questions.takeaway: An attached internet gateway is used only after a route table routes 0.0.0.0/0 to it for the associated subnets.

read.text: Attaching alone does not yet tell instances how to reach the internet.

questions.stem: The cafe attached an internet gateway to its VPC, and the web servers in its public subnets already have public IPv4 addresses. The servers still cannot reach the internet. What is missing?

options.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route in a table associated with the subnets
options.why: The route sends internet traffic to the gateway, and the association applies that route to the public subnets.

options.text: The auto-assign public IPv4 setting turned on for the public subnets
options.why: The servers already have public addresses, so this setting is not what keeps them off the internet.

options.text: A local route that lets the resources inside the VPC reach one another
options.why: Every route table starts with the local route, and it only carries traffic inside the VPC.

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway acting as a hub between the VPC and other cafe networks
options.why: Transit Gateway links VPCs and on-premises networks; it gives the public subnets no route to the internet.

notes.title: More Ways to Connect to the AWS Cloud

lines: Client VPN links people on their own devices, while Site-to-Site VPN links a whole office or shop network to the VPC.
Direct Connect is a dedicated private line worth choosing only when heavy traffic needs the bandwidth, and a VPN tunnel can stand by if its cable is cut.
Transit Gateway joins many networks at one hub, while PrivateLink opens private access to exactly the services the cafe chooses.
An internet gateway carries traffic both ways between the VPC and the internet, while a NAT gateway lets private servers call out but not be called.

questions.takeaway: Huge transfers and lasting hybrid apps that outgrow shared links call for a dedicated Direct Connect line.

read.text: Shared links can jam, so Direct Connect gives a dedicated private line from your network to a VPC (via a Direct Connect location and a virtual private gateway), cutting costs and raising bandwidth.

questions.stem: The cafe chain is moving years of security camera video and nightly backups to AWS, and will keep some apps on premises for good. Its shared internet links already jam during transfers. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
options.why: Site-to-Site VPN runs over shared links, so it does not add the bandwidth these large transfers need.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.why: Direct Connect gives a dedicated private line with more bandwidth for huge transfers and lasting hybrid apps.

options.text: AWS Client VPN
options.why: Client VPN connects individual people, and it does not raise bandwidth for bulk data moves.

options.text: AWS PrivateLink
options.why: PrivateLink gives a VPC private access to services, not a dedicated line from the cafe's network.

questions.takeaway: Private access to one chosen service in another VPC, with no public IP, points to AWS PrivateLink.

read.text: For resources: highly available, scalable private access from a VPC to services as if they were inside it, including other VPCs, other clouds and on-premises networks.

questions.stem: The cafe's ordering app runs in its VPC and must call a bakery supplier's stock service that lives in another VPC. The cafe wants to reach only that one service, with no public IP addresses on either side. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS Transit Gateway
options.why: Transit Gateway is a hub that joins whole networks, rather than exposing one chosen service privately.

options.text: NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances call out to outside hosts, which sends traffic beyond the VPC.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.why: Direct Connect is a dedicated line from an on-premises network, not private access to one service in a VPC.

options.text: AWS PrivateLink
options.why: PrivateLink gives private access to a chosen service in another VPC as if it were local, with no public IP.

questions.takeaway: A NAT gateway fits private servers that must call out to the internet, such as to fetch a supplier's files, while blocking calls in.

read.text: NAT gateway: private instances can start outside connections, but outsiders cannot start ones to them.

questions.stem: The cafe's admin plans to add a NAT gateway to the VPC. Which of the cafe's needs would it meet?

options.text: Baristas working from home must join the VPC from their laptops
options.why: Staff joining the VPC from their own laptops need AWS Client VPN, while a NAT gateway only lets private instances call out.

options.text: Private stock servers must fetch price lists from a supplier's site
options.why: A NAT gateway lets the private stock servers start the fetch from the supplier's site, and outsiders still cannot start connections to them.

options.text: Two branch cafes must link their networks to the VPC over encryption
options.why: Encrypted links from branch sites to the VPC come from AWS Site-to-Site VPN, which a NAT gateway does not provide.

options.text: The cafe's several VPCs must all connect through one central hub
options.why: A central hub joining many VPCs is AWS Transit Gateway, while a NAT gateway only gives private instances a way out.

incidents.title: Ordering site dark after the rebuild
incidents.brief: The cafe rebuilt its online ordering site in a fresh VPC over the weekend. On Monday morning no customer can open it, and the manager wants it back before the lunch orders start.

steps.takeaway: A subnet turns public through its route to an attached internet gateway, never through its name.

read.text: Naming a subnet "public" does not make it public, because it still needs an attached internet gateway and a route to it.

steps.stem: The cafe put its ordering servers in a subnet it named public-orders, yet no request from the internet reaches them. A teammate says the name alone already makes the subnet public. Which fact about a subnet is what actually makes it public?

options.text: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to an attached internet gateway
options.why: Traffic leaves a subnet by its routes, so a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an attached internet gateway is what opens it to the internet.

options.text: Its auto-assign setting gives each new server a public IPv4 address
options.why: Public subnets do switch this on, but a public address alone gets no request through without a route to an internet gateway.

options.text: Its route table keeps traffic inside the VPC with a local route
options.why: Every route table starts with this local route, and it only carries traffic within the VPC, never to the internet.

options.text: A NAT gateway lets its servers start connections to the outside
options.why: A NAT gateway lets servers call out but blocks connections started outside, so customers still cannot reach them.

steps.takeaway: An unedited default network ACL allows all traffic both ways, while a custom one denies everything until you add rules.

read.text: Every AWS account comes with a default network ACL that lets everything through until you edit its rules.

steps.stem: The cafe's ordering servers now sit in a subnet with a working route to the internet, but customers' requests still fail. The subnet is still on the network ACL that AWS gave the account at the start, untouched since then. Which fact settles whether that network ACL is what turns the customers away?

options.text: The default network ACL lets all traffic in and out until edited
options.why: An unedited default network ACL allows every request in and every reply out, so it is not what turns the customers away.

options.text: A custom network ACL blocks all traffic until allow rules are added
options.why: This is true of a custom network ACL, but the ACL an account starts with is the default one, so it does not apply here.

options.text: Every network ACL ends in an explicit deny rule for unmatched packets
options.why: The default network ACL's allow rules match every packet first, so its final deny rule never reaches the customers' requests.

options.text: A network ACL rechecks each reply with no memory of the request
options.why: Being stateless means replies are checked again, yet the default network ACL allows them out, so this blocks nothing.

steps.takeaway: A new security group denies all inbound and allows all outbound traffic, so a web server needs an inbound allow rule.

read.text: Out of the box it blocks every inbound port and sender address and lets all outbound traffic go.

steps.stem: The cafe's ordering servers have a working route and an open subnet, yet they still turn every customer away. Their security group still has exactly the settings it was given at launch. Which behavior of that security group turns the customers away?

options.text: It denies all inbound traffic until allow rules are added
options.why: A new security group blocks every inbound port and sender until the cafe opens it with allow rules, such as one for HTTPS.

options.text: It lets all outbound traffic leave without an allow rule
options.why: Open outbound traffic is true of a new security group, but it lets traffic leave and turns no customer away.

options.text: It lets replies back in for requests the server sent out
options.why: Being stateful passes replies to the server's own requests, which helps traffic through rather than blocking customers.

options.text: It filters traffic for one instance, not the whole subnet
options.why: Working at the instance level is true of a security group, but its scope alone says nothing about what it blocks.

options.text: AWS PrivateLink

steps.stem: The bean shop's sale pages mix fixed product photos with prices and stock counts that change all day. The cafe wants both kinds of content handed to shoppers from locations near them, instead of from the one Region. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront
options.why: CloudFront is a CDN that serves both static and dynamic web content from edge locations close to each shopper.

options.text: Amazon Route 53
options.why: Route 53 answers DNS lookups and routes users, but it does not hand them content from nearby locations.

options.text: AWS Global Accelerator
options.why: Global Accelerator carries traffic over the AWS network to healthy endpoints, but it does not serve copies of content near users.

options.text: AWS Direct Connect
options.why: Direct Connect is a private line from a data center to a VPC, and it does nothing for shoppers far from the Region.

steps.takeaway: To send each user to the Region that answers with the lowest delay, choose Route 53 latency-based routing.

read.text: Routing policies: weighted round robin, latency-based, geolocation and geoproximity.

steps.stem: The cafe adds a second copy of its bean shop in a European Region. It wants Route 53 to send each shopper to whichever Region answers that shopper with the least delay, wherever the shopper lives. Which routing policy fits?

options.text: Latency-based routing
options.why: Latency-based routing picks the Region that gives each user the lowest delay, which is exactly the cafe's goal.

options.text: Geolocation routing
options.why: Geolocation routing decides by the country or area a shopper is in, not by which Region answers faster.

options.text: Weighted round robin routing
options.why: Weighted round robin splits traffic between endpoints by set shares, whatever delay each shopper sees.

options.text: Geoproximity routing
options.why: Geoproximity routing works from geography, not from which Region answers each shopper with the least delay.

steps.takeaway: Route 53 health checks let DNS steer users away from endpoints that stop responding.

read.text: It also runs health checks, registers new domains and takes over DNS records from other registrars, so all your domains live in one place.

steps.stem: The cafe's bean shop runs in two Regions, and during the sale one of them sometimes stops answering. The cafe wants Route 53 to keep probing each copy of the shop, so that shoppers are sent only to a copy that still responds. Which Route 53 feature fits?

options.text: Name resolution
options.why: Resolving the shop's name hands back an address, but on its own it never tests whether that copy still responds.

options.text: Latency-based routing
options.why: Latency-based routing picks the Region with the least delay for each shopper, not whether that Region still answers.

options.text: Health checks
options.why: Route 53 health checks keep probing each endpoint, so its DNS answers can leave out a copy that stops responding.

options.text: Geolocation routing
options.why: Geolocation routing sends shoppers by where they are, with no test of whether the chosen copy still answers.

incidents.title: Stock counts stop flowing in the new VPC
incidents.brief: The cafe built a separate VPC for its new inventory system, with order servers in a public subnet and inventory servers in a private one. Stock counts have stopped updating, and the kitchen lead wants them flowing again before the next delivery.

steps.takeaway: A route table's local route keeps traffic inside the VPC, so its subnets reach each other with no extra routes.

read.text: Its Routes tab starts with a single local route that keeps traffic inside the VPC.

steps.stem: The cafe's order servers in a public subnet send stock updates to its inventory servers in a private subnet of the same VPC. Which route in the private subnet's route table carries that traffic?

options.text: A local route for the VPC's own range
options.why: Every route table starts with a local route that keeps traffic inside the VPC, so it carries updates between two subnets of one VPC.

options.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway
options.why: A route to the internet gateway sends traffic out to the internet, and it would also make the inventory subnet public.

options.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route to a NAT gateway
options.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances call out to the internet, not receive updates from another subnet of the VPC.

options.text: A route to the order subnet via a transit gateway
options.why: Transit Gateway links whole VPCs and on-premises networks, and two subnets of one VPC already reach each other without it.

steps.takeaway: Security group rules reuse CIDR notation to name the address ranges that traffic may come from or go to.

read.text: Next comes traffic filtering through security groups and network ACLs, and security groups reuse CIDR notation to define where traffic may come from or go to.

steps.stem: The cafe's new VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16, and its order servers sit in a public subnet with 10.0.3.0/24. The security group on the inventory servers must admit stock updates from that subnet only. Which source should the security group rule name?

options.why: Security groups use CIDR notation for a traffic source, and 10.0.3.0/24 is exactly the order subnet's address range.
This range covers the whole VPC, so the rule would admit traffic from every subnet, not only the order subnet.
This range matches every address, so the rule would admit traffic from anywhere, including the internet.
This range belongs to a different subnet of the VPC, so it would miss the order servers entirely.

steps.takeaway: Several instances can share one security group, so identical rules need not be rebuilt for each new server.

read.text: Instances in one VPC can share a security group or each use their own.

steps.stem: With stock counts flowing again, the cafe adds more inventory servers beside the first one, and each needs exactly the rules its security group already holds. Which fact about security groups lets the cafe do this without writing the rules again?

options.text: A security group can be shared by several instances
options.why: Several instances can use one security group, so the new servers can be given the group the first server already uses.

options.text: A security group lets all outbound traffic go by default
options.why: This is true of a new security group, but it says nothing about giving several servers the same rules.

options.text: A security group remembers requests and admits their replies
options.why: This stateful behavior is true, but it only handles replies and does not copy rules to the new servers.

options.text: A security group holds allow rules only, with no deny rules
options.why: This is true of security groups, but the kind of rule they hold does not spread those rules to other servers.
